opus-5.5.text:
I think product impact matters a lot, and it's something my thinking on has changed over time.

Early on, especially coming from a research background, I was mostly driven by curiosity: is this an interesting problem, is it elegant, does it push the frontier of what we understand? That's still very important to me. But over the last few years I've come to feel that in AI, research and product are no longer two separate worlds. The most important research questions are increasingly *defined* by what happens when real people use these systems.

When a model is deployed and millions of people interact with it, you get a kind of signal you just can't get from benchmarks. Benchmarks are useful, but they're proxies, and once everyone optimizes for them, they saturate and stop telling you much. Real usage tells you where the model actually fails, what people actually need, and what "intelligence" means in practice. So for me, product impact is a source of truth for research, not just a downstream result.

There's also a values question. If you're working on something as powerful as AI, I think you should care whether it actually makes people's lives better. A paper that gets cited is nice, but seeing something you worked on help someone do their job, learn something, or solve a problem they couldn't before is a different kind of satisfaction. It keeps you honest.

That said, I don't think product impact should be the *only* criterion. If you chase short-term product metrics too much, you can end up making incremental improvements and missing the bigger shifts. Some of the most important work looks useless at first. So the balance I try to strike is: pick problems that I believe will eventually matter a lot for how people use AI, even if the payoff isn't immediate, and stay close enough to real usage that I'm not fooling myself about what matters.

So in one sentence: I see product impact as the ultimate test of whether the research was right, but not as a replacement for having a long-term research taste.

r001.rationale: He describes a shift over time: early in his career he was mainly driven by research curiosity, while in recent years product impact has become a key source of truth for research.

fable-5.1.text:
I think product impact matters a lot to me now, but it wasn't always the thing I optimized for. When I was doing my PhD at Princeton, the metric in my head was mostly intellectual: is this idea new, does it change how people think about the problem. Papers like ReAct or Tree of Thoughts came out of that mindset. I wasn't thinking "millions of people will use this," I was thinking "this is the right way to frame how a language model should reason and act."

What changed my view is seeing how those ideas actually traveled. ReAct didn't matter because it was a paper, it mattered because it became the default pattern inside LangChain and basically every agent framework after it. SWE-bench didn't matter because of the leaderboard itself, it mattered because it gave every lab a concrete target that reshaped what "coding agent" even meant. So in retrospect the research that I'm proudest of is exactly the research that ended up in products, and I don't think that's a coincidence.

The way I'd put it now is that in this field, the gap between research and product has almost collapsed. In the pre-training era you could do a clever paper and it would take years to show up anywhere. In the agent era, if your idea is right, someone ships it within months, and if nobody ships it, that's actually a signal that the idea might not be as important as you thought. Product is the fastest feedback loop we have on whether a research direction is real.

I also think the second half of AI, as I like to call it, is less about inventing new methods and more about defining the right problems and the right environments. And you can't define the right problems from inside a lab. You need to see where real users get stuck, where agents fail in ways that no benchmark captures. That's why I moved toward working closer to actual systems people use. It's not that I care less about ideas. It's that the ideas worth having are now downstream of contact with reality.

So yes, product impact is very important to me, but I'd frame it less as "I want to build products" and more as "I want to work on problems where the answer gets tested by the world, not just by reviewers."

r001.rationale: He says product impact matters a lot to him now, but that during his Princeton PhD he mainly optimized for intellectual novelty and framing. This clearly describes a shift across career stages.

astra-6.text:
For me, product impact is an important part of deciding what’s worth working on. A research result can be interesting on its own, but I also want to understand what it enables someone to do. Does it solve a problem they actually have? Does it make something useful possible that wasn’t possible before?

That doesn’t mean every research project needs an immediate product application. Some ideas need time, and it can be hard to predict where they’ll become useful. But I like having a connection between the research question and a real-world need. When people use a system, you learn which capabilities matter, where it breaks, and which assumptions were wrong. That feedback can lead to better research questions.

So I see product impact as both a motivation and a way to learn. Ultimately, I’d like the work to turn into something people find valuable in their lives.

r001.rationale: The response describes product impact as a motivation and a way to learn, but does not say its importance varies with Shunyu Yao’s career stage.

sol-6.1.text:
I think product impact is a very important part of what makes research meaningful to me. You can develop a new method and show that it improves a benchmark, but there’s still a gap between that and making something people actually find useful. Closing that gap can reveal research questions that you wouldn’t discover by looking at benchmarks alone.

For me, the interesting thing is the connection between the two. Research expands what’s possible, and building products helps you understand which capabilities matter and where the limitations really are. I wouldn’t say every research project needs an immediate application, but I do want the work I pursue, over time, to translate into something that helps people.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes product impact as important to him and says he wants his work to translate into useful applications over time, but it does not say that its importance varies by career stage.
